doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Erroll Garner and the bass players
summary: Praise for Garner's improvised introductions and for never telling the bassist the key, and how bassists watched his left hand according to a biography.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: important, to be in the moment. You know, don’t go — in my opinion, I don’t want to go on stage with a preconceived set list that is going to happen, this and this and this. Because it takes away all the fun of it. The most beautiful feeling is when you get in front of the piano and the audience and you are blank. And you have to figure out what’s the right tune to play to make the people happy and yourself happy. And this was the approach that some of the greatest players used. I mean think of Errol Garner. Errol Garner never went on stage knowing what he was going to play you know. In fact, all those crazy introductions that he used to make up, he needed to do that to make up his mind what he was going to be playing. And the result was the audience went crazy because the audience would hear this completely far out introduction and then all of a sudden “I’m Confessing That I Love You” or one of those great songs. And it’s beautiful. I mean it’s beautiful. What can I say? It’s beautiful. And one of the most fun of Errol Garner [habits] had was never tell the bass player which key you were going to play a song. And sometimes the night before he would play a certain song in E flat. And then two nights later he would play again the same song, I don’t know, in A major. And the bass player, to figure out. And now on YouTube you see all these videos and you can spot on these videos that he’s pleased with the fact that the bass player is just fishing around for the right chord you know. Nothing wrong with that. That’s the beauty. Because jazz is about hearing, it’s about connecting, it’s about having fun. That’s the way I see it.

I can’t think of a better way to say it. That was fantastic what you just said. I wonder how the bass players used to talk amongst themselves about, “hey have you played with Errol? What was that like for you?”

Yeah. In fact you know there is only that I know one biography of Errol Garner. And he never, I think very seldom he did an interview. So this biography was put together by collecting what other people who worked with Errol and knew Errol had to say about him. And so this is what all the bass players that appear in this book, they say all the same thing, that they had to stand right there by the left hand. You know the piano is here and the bass player is standing there, because they had to try to catch what he was doing with the left hand whenever their ear wouldn’t be fast enough. So they would look at — but then of course Errol would use, sometimes, voicings with the left hand where not necessarily the lower note was the note that the bass player is supposed to play. So the bass player is supposed to have some, also, kind of piano knowledge, to know that if he was playing a certain voicing, let’s say with an A with the pinky, the lowest note, they were supposed to play an F for example, or, you know, things like that. It’s very interesting. Very nice. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
